verdicts.reason: Mainstream in 2007, 3 to 5 years after the placed year 2004. Neither builder. A's 2006 is contradicted by Nokia's figures: 133M Bluetooth phones in 2005 against a handset market of about 780M (~17%), 220M forecast for 2006 (well under half globally). Mainstream in 2002, placed year 2001: within 2 years after, or earlier. Builder A was closer. Jupiter Research (reported by InfoWorld, January 2004) found 80% of companies surveyed had already deployed portals or planned to deploy them soon; Forrester 2006 found 46% of large companies using an employee portal. Packaged portal products date from 1998. The 20% crossing among large and medium organisations is therefore no later than 2006 and most likely by 2002-2003, given the deployed-or-planned share at the end of 2003. An Answerthink survey (October 2002) reported in pass 1 as more than 50% of companies with portals could not be opened. 2002 is kept as an estimate inside the bound; the placed year 2001 needs mainstream by 2003 for a hit, so the verdict rests on that estimate with medium-low certainty. Builder B's 2004 interpolated from the 2006 figure without an earlier data point. year_5pct 1999 is a bound (packaged products from 1998).

Mainstream in 2006, placed year 2004: within 2 years after, or earlier. Builder A's verdicts stand but on a different test. A used IP-capable PBX line shipments (hybrid lines are not VoIP use), B used US residential voice connections only. France is a major market: ARCEP counted about 6.6M broadband-voice subscriptions at end 2006 (about a quarter of ~26M households) and 10.8M at end 2007 (27.4% of all phone subscriptions), adding about a million a quarter, so the 20% line was passed in 2006. In-Stat/MDR: US businesses using VoIP 3% (2003) to 12% (2004), so 5% in 2004. B's error: restricting the denominator to the US and missing France/Japan, which crossed 2-3 years earlier. Enterprise use alone was slower: Forrester counted IP PBXs at 14% of North American enterprises in 2006 and 23% in 2007, hosted VoIP 3% and 8%. year_mainstream is precise to about a year; 2006 vs 2007 only changes the 1999 claim (P=2004).

Pew fact sheet confirms US home broadband 6-9% (2001), 15-19% (2003), 23-26% (2004), so US-only gives mainstream 2004 = P+3. But StatCan The Daily 23 Sep 2003: 2.8 million Canadian households had broadband in 2001 (about 24% of ~11.6M households), and builder B itself notes Korea passed 20% around 2001; under the one-major-market test both builders used for Smart Cards, mainstream by P=2001: hit.

Mainstream in 2004, placed year 2004: within 2 years after, or earlier. Closer to A. year_mainstream 2004 is an upper bound (no later than 2004), which is all the 1999 claim (placed 2004, hit if mainstream by 2006) needs. GAO-04-548 (May 2004) found 52 of 128 surveyed US federal agencies using or planning data mining, with 199 efforts of which 131 were operational: well above 20% of a large-organisation population by 2004, and the commercial heavy users (credit scoring, telecom churn, retail basket analysis) were earlier than government. B's 2014 used the wrong denominator and object: TDWI/Eurostat measure predictive analytics or big-data analysis across all companies of all sizes, a later and broader technology, not data mining among organisations with large customer databases. A's evidence (Wikipedia) carries no share figure, so the year rests on the GAO count. Low-to-moderate certainty.

Mainstream in 2015, 3 to 5 years after the placed year 2010. Revised in pass 2; follows the DMG data. Reading and test as pass 1 (contact-centre speech analytics). DMG Consulting counted 25 commercial implementations in 2004 and 1,764 at end-2008, forecast 40-45% growth a year for 2009-2011 and at least 25-30% of all contact-centre seats within five to seven years (2014-2016). DMG's 2015-2016 report counts 2,889,031 speech-analytics seats in May 2014 and 3,507,795 in March 2015. Against a world base of roughly 12-17 million contact-centre seats, that is about 17-24% in 2014 and 20-29% in 2015, so the 20% crossing is set at 2015 (bounded 2014-2016). Back-casting the seat count at 30-40% growth puts 5% of seats at about 2010, so year_5pct 2010 stays. Pass 1's 2012 rested on a ContactBabel figure (24% of contact-centre organisations in 2012) that could not be found on any opened page. The builders' 2019 has no data point. For the 2000 claim (placed 2010) both 2012 and 2015 are within reach of the rule only as: 5% by the placed year (partial) or mainstream 5 years after (partial); a hit would need 20% by 2012, which the opened sources do not show.

Reached 5% only in 2005; not mainstream by 2007 (placed year 2002 plus 5). Neither builder. Pass 1 dated mainstream to 2009 from Forrester's software survey (Q4 2009, published 2010: 25% of North American companies using SaaS); that page is now dead (404) and the figure could not be re-confirmed. The opened Eurostat release bounds it: in 2014, 19% of all EU enterprises with 10+ staff bought cloud services (mostly SaaS: e-mail, files, office software), and large enterprises (250+) were at about 35% (56% in 2018 after a 21-point rise since 2014). So 20% of organisations in a major market is reached no later than 2014 for large firms; 2009 lies inside that bound and is kept. B's 2016 used the all-enterprise EU average including 10-49 staff firms. year_5pct 2005 is an estimate (no measured series before 2007); the 2000 claim (P=2002) is a miss under any year_5pct after 2002, which no source supports. Verdicts: 2000 claim miss, 2001 claim partial. Low-to-moderate certainty: a mainstream year of 2012 or later together with a 5% year after 2006 would turn the 2001 claim into a miss.

Mainstream in 2013, placed year 2011: within 2 years after, or earlier. Neither builder; closer to A. Mainstream in 2011, 3 to 5 years after the placed year 2006. Builder B. A applied the 50%-of-new-units device-feature test globally (crossed 2013), but a PDA phone is a device class bought by users, so D16's 20%-of-target-users test fits; Pew measured 35% of US adults owning a smartphone in 2011, so 2011 is an upper bound (comScore-type subscriber data suggest 2010). Smartphones were above 5% of global phone sales by 2006 (estimate; builder B's figure of about 10% in 2007 was not re-confirmed on an opened page). Any year_mainstream from 2010 to 2011 gives partial for both claims (placed 2006 and 2007); only a crossing by 2009 would turn the 2002 claim into a hit, and Pew's first measure (35% in 2011) with US smartphone ownership rising fast from about 2009 makes 2010-2011 the likely crossing.

Mainstream in 2005, placed year 2003: within 2 years after, or earlier. Follows B. Mainstream in 2004, placed year 2003: within 2 years after, or earlier. Builder A was closer. In 2003, the year Centrino launched (March 2003, with integrated Intel PRO/Wireless), In-Stat/MDR counted about 16 million Wi-Fi-enabled notebooks sold to businesses and Strategy Analytics about 8 million worldwide, against roughly 40 million notebooks shipped (20-40%). Analysts forecast integrated WLAN in 95% (In-Stat/MDR, 2005), 90% (Strategy Analytics, 2008) and 80% (Forrester, 2008) of notebooks; by 2005 the majority of Intel Mobility Group revenue came from Centrino, which includes the Wi-Fi radio. Half of new notebooks is reached in 2004 or 2005 at the latest. Builder B used a household test without early household data and set 2006 by estimate; households are not the dominant target on an enterprise-oriented chart, and the device-feature test is the one D16 names for a built-in radio. 2004 is an estimate inside the 2004-2005 bound; only placed year 2003 matters (hit if mainstream by 2005), so the verdict holds either way.

At least 5% from 2006, below mainstream by the placed year 2007 (mainstream only in 2014). Neither builder: both flagged the label ambiguous, but one reading dominates on a 2002 Emerging Technologies chart. Vehicle toll tags were mature by 2002 (Telepass 1989, E-ZPass in the 1990s) and electronic shelf labels were 1990s technology, so neither fits a label placed 2-5 years from the plateau. Supply-chain RFID tags were the emerging-technology story of 2002 (Auto-ID Center, EPC, the Gillette order of early 2003). Under that reading, mandated case and pallet tagging by Walmart's top suppliers (2005, about 600 suppliers by 2007), Metro and the US DoD put routine use above 5% of the relevant retail and CPG supplier population around 2006. Surveys still describe adoption as early-stage in 2007, and by 2015 a GS1 US / Auburn survey found 57% of retailers and 48% of manufacturers implementing EPC RFID, with 40-47% of apparel and general-merchandise items tagged. The mainstream year is an estimate, bounded after 2009, which is all the 2002 claim (placed 2007, partial unless mainstream by 2009) needs. year_5pct 2006 is low-to-moderate certainty. If the evidence showed under 5% by 2007, the claim would be a miss.

Mainstream in 2011, 3 to 5 years after the placed year 2007. Builder B's verdict (partial), but via an earlier mainstream year, not via B's 2002 5% year. Both builders guessed 2013 without evidence. Janrain's Social Identity study by Blue Research (US consumers, reported January 2012) found that 41% of social media users chose social login to sign in to websites in 2011, up from 28% in 2010 (77% said sites should offer it). With Facebook alone at 54% of US adults in 2012 (Pew), about two-thirds of internet users, that is roughly a quarter of US internet users, so mainstream by 2011. This is a vendor-commissioned survey that measures the preferred sign-in method, so 2011 has low-medium confidence; it is within P+5 (2012) by one year. B's year_5pct 2002 counted Passport accounts used mostly on Microsoft's own services, which is not third-party sign-in: eBay and Monster cancelled their Passport agreements in 2004. year_5pct 2009 is an estimate (social login at 28% of social media users in 2010) and does not affect the verdict.

At least 5% from 2001, below mainstream by the placed year 2007 (mainstream only in 2013). Closer to A. Both builders define the label as 'Ask Jeeves style', so Ask Jeeves usage counts toward the 5% floor. comScore Media Metrix put Ask Jeeves sites at about 6% of US searches through July 2004 and 6.1% in July 2005 (with its acquired engines); Ask Jeeves alone was about 2-3.5% of searches. Its share of searchers (monthly reach) was higher than its share of queries, so 5% of searchers is met no later than 2004-2005; 2001 is kept as the pass-1 value inside that bound. B's 2019 (BERT) moves the test to back-end language understanding on Google and ignores the Ask Jeeves base that B's own reading names. year_mainstream: Hummingbird 2013 (A) or BERT 2019-20 (B); both are later than 2012, so the 2002 claim (placed 2007) is a partial either way. Only the 5% year decides it, and every candidate year is before 2007.

Mainstream in 2006, placed year 2012: within 2 years after, or earlier. Builder A was closer, on reading rather than on retrieved data. No survey with an organisation share was found (three searches in pass 1 and 2). The call rests on the shape of the market: Celent (February 2006) judged that grid computing in financial services had 'finally hit the tipping point', changing how firms model risk, with grid spending forecast to rise from just over US$100 million to nearly US$500 million between 2006 and 2010; grid-scheduled compute farms were also routine at pharma and chip designers, and the practice continued into HPC clusters and cloud rather than being abandoned. Builder B left mainstream null for lack of evidence, which grades the absence of a survey as the absence of adoption; that is the wrong default when the relevant industry plainly runs the technology. year_mainstream 2006 is an estimate; for the claims it only needs to be no later than 2012 (placed years 2010, 2011, 2012), which is the confident part. Low certainty on the exact year.

Abandoned in 2013 without reaching mainstream within 5 years after the placed year 2012. Builder A. B's two readings are not equally faithful: consumer file sharing was already mass-market in 2002 (Kazaa), so Gartner placing 'Peer-to-peer computing' 5-10 years from the plateau only makes sense for the enterprise computing model, which is what an Emerging Technologies chart addresses. The enterprise model never showed a measured 5% share; its flagship product (Groove, Microsoft Office Groove, SharePoint Workspace 2010) was dropped from Office 2013 in favour of cloud sync. Abandoned year 2013 (A had ~2015); either gives miss for P=2012.

At least 5% from 2000, below mainstream by the placed year 2007 (mainstream only in 2017). Follows B. A's denominator is wrong: 'websites serving HTTPS by default' measures the web-TLS end state, not organisations deploying PKI. It led A to a 5% year of 2013, although SSL server certificates for e-commerce and large government PKIs (the DoD Common Access Card from 2001) put organisational use well above 5% by 2000-2002. The mainstream year is a late bound. Enterprise PKI with user certificates was widely judged a disappointment through the 2000s, and no survey found shows 20% of organisations running it routinely by 2009 (the hit threshold for the 2002 claim placed at 2007). The 2015-2017 HTTPS shift is the first clearly evidenced mass use. Low certainty on the upper side: if an organisation holding any SSL certificate counted as 'using PKI', the crossing would be in the 2000s and the verdict a hit. Search found no 2006-2008 survey to settle it.

Mainstream in 2011, 3 to 5 years after the placed year 2008. Builder B was closer, narrowly. Forrester reported in July 2008 that the number of UC trials at firms had jumped more than 20% in a year but with little conversion into actual deployments, and did not expect full deployments within the next year; its Q1 2008 European data had 81% of enterprises 'at some stage' of UC implementation, which counts plans and pilots, and builder A's own 2009 Forrester figure is 22% of enterprises 'implemented or implementing', which includes projects still in progress. Production use by 20% therefore lands after 2009, most likely 2010-2011; Infonetics described VoIP services (with hosted UC growing) as mainstream in many developed countries by 2012. A took the implemented-or-implementing figure as production use one year later; that overcounts. 2011 is an estimate within 2010-2012; the 2003 claim (placed 2008) is a hit only if the crossing is 2010, so that call is close; the 2004 claim (placed 2009) is a hit at 2011.

Mainstream in 2008, placed year 2008: within 2 years after, or earlier. Builder B's verdict (hit), with an earlier year. Both builders looked only at the US SEC phase-in (2009-2011). A's 2011 was a wrong-market error. Any year up to 2010 gives hit for P=2008; China's exchanges mandated XBRL even earlier (2004-2005, not retrieved).

B's own Pew 35% figure contradicts its choice of 2011 as the first year. Abandoned in 2009 without reaching mainstream within 5 years after the placed year 2014. Builder B. Gartner's label deliberately isolates the case/pallet application. The retail mandates stalled in 2007-2009 and Walmart moved to item-level tagging (apparel, later home goods and hardlines); the later RFID growth (GS1 US 2015 survey: 47% of goods received by RFID-aware retailers tagged) is item-level source tagging, which is a different application. A kept it 'not abandoned' on the strength of DoD and niche logistics use, but gave no evidence of a sustained 5% share of the relevant suppliers after 2009; even the 5% year is generous (a few hundred mandated suppliers out of tens of thousands). Any of 'abandoned 2009' or 'never reached 5%' gives miss for all five claims (P=2014-2019); abandoned year approximate.

Mainstream in 2011, placed year 2009: within 2 years after, or earlier. Follows A. Pew's 2011 location-based services report (May 2011 survey) found 28% of US cell owners using their phone for directions or recommendations based on location. That is about 23% of all adults, already above 20% in 2011. B used the 2013 Pew figure (74% of smartphone owners) and an ownership ramp to date the crossing at 2012, without checking the 2011 Pew measure. The crossing may have happened in 2010, so 2011 is an upper bound. That is enough for the 2004 claim placed at 2009: a hit needs mainstream by 2011.

Mainstream in 2006, placed year 2006: within 2 years after, or earlier. Builder A was closer, consistent with the grid-computing call. Internal compute grids (Platform LSF/Symphony, DataSynapse, Sun Grid Engine, United Devices Grid MP) were the practical, adopted part of the grid wave: grid-scheduled compute farms were routine at large banks, chip designers and pharma by the mid-2000s, and the practice continued as HPC clusters and then cloud. Builder B agreed on the practice but set mainstream null for want of a survey; absence of a published share is not evidence of non-adoption when the relevant industry plainly ran it. No survey found (shared with grid-computing searches). 2006 is an estimate; placed year 2006 needs mainstream by 2008 for a hit, so a crossing as late as 2008 gives the same verdict. Low certainty.

Mainstream in 2007, placed year 2015: within 2 years after, or earlier. Builder B. A called the label ambiguous, but Gartner's description of collective intelligence at the time (group knowledge produced with no central authority, enabled by wikis and Web 2.0) gives a dominant reading, and its main forms (Wikipedia, enterprise wikis, user ratings) were all mainstream well before P+2=2017; only the narrow prediction-market reading would fail, and it did not dominate. Pew: 36% of US online adults consulted Wikipedia in Feb 2007, 53% in 2010. Any year before 2017 gives hit for P=2015.

At least 5% from 2006, below mainstream by the placed year 2015. Follows B. A's 'no measurable 5% share' is wrong. The Torchiano et al. 2012-13 survey of 155 Italian software professionals (online questionnaire February-April 2011) reports that of 155 respondents 105 model (13% always, 55% sometimes) and 44% of those 105 modellers use code generation, 16% model interpretation; so about 30% of all respondents (46 of 155) use code generation at least sometimes. With a self-selected sample and occasional use, that is still clearly above 5% before 2015, and model-based code generation was routine in automotive and embedded work from the mid-2000s. A judged the 5% floor from the Wikipedia statement that MDA never gained 'mainstream industry acceptance', which concerns 20%, not 5%. Mainstream stays null. The same survey finds only 13% of companies model 'always' and models used mainly for documentation, and the MDE literature reports low industrial adoption, so routine model-driven generation by 20% of software organisations is not shown by 2021 (the latest hit year for the claims). year_5pct 2006 is an estimate; it is bounded at no later than 2011 by the survey date. Risk: if the ~30% of respondents using code generation is read as routine use by organisations, the verdict would rise to hit.

Mainstream in 2016, placed year 2015: within 2 years after, or earlier. Neither builder on years; the verdict follows A. Functional inkjet reached volume in display manufacturing, which is the relevant industry (builder B's printed-electronics denominator, still mostly prototyping, is the wrong one). Two uses: inkjet thin-film encapsulation for flexible OLED, which debuted in manufacturing in 2014 and by September 2016 had won 'the vast majority of available TFE orders' from the largest panel makers in three Asian regions (Kateeva, Semiconductor Digest); and inkjet coating of polyimide alignment layers in LCD fabs, which a BOE patent filed in 2016-2017 describes as 'recently applied in an inkjet manner, which gradually replaces a conventional coating manner'. Pass 1 put mainstream at 2012 on the claim that every major panel maker ran inkjet PI lines by 2010-2012; that claim rested on a search summary and the BOE text contradicts it (still 'recently' and 'gradually' in 2016). Routine inkjet use by at least 20% of the large panel makers is therefore set at 2016, when inkjet TFE had most of the market and inkjet PI was spreading at BOE and others. year_5pct 2008 is kept as an estimate (early inkjet PI and colour-filter use; no figure fixes it). The 2005 claim (placed 2015) is a hit for any mainstream year up to 2017, so the verdict is unchanged. Medium-low certainty.
